text: Chapter 1 kept returning to one rule — a model must be judged on data it has not seen. In practice that means deciding, before you fit anything, which rows are for learning and which are for judging. This lesson shows how to split data properly, and the small choices that separate an honest evaluation from a misleading one.

Three sets, three jobs. Training set — the rows the model learns from, fit sees only these. Validation set — rows used to compare models and choose settings, you can look at these scores as many times as you like. Test set — a final, one-time check of the chosen model, since you never tuned anything against it, its score is an honest estimate of real performance. A common split is 60-20-20, or 70-15-15 for smaller datasets.
Using 500 illustrative customers with a churn flag — churn is uncommon here, an imbalanced target, exactly where splitting needs care. The overall churn rate comes out to 0.09 across 500 rows.

A plain random split can, by bad luck, put too many or too few churners in the test set — with only about 45 churners total, that swing is large. A plain split here gave a test churn rate of 13 percent against a true 9 percent. Passing stratify equals y forces every split to keep the same class proportions, and the stratified test set matched exactly at 9 percent.

To see how much luck is involved, repeating both plain and stratified splits across 300 different seeds and measuring each test set's churn rate: the plain split's standard deviation is 0.0253, wandering by about two and a half points, while the stratified split's standard deviation is exactly 0 — pinned to the true rate every single time.

train_test_split only makes two pieces, so call it twice for a three-way split — first carve off the test set, then split the remainder into train and validation. Because 0.25 of the remaining 80 percent is 20 percent of the total, this gives exactly 60, 20, and 20 — 300, 100, and 100 rows here.

A random split assumes rows are interchangeable, which fails in two common situations. Time-ordered data — if you'll predict the future, the test set must come from after the training set, so sort by date and cut, rather than randomly mixing dates and letting the model peek at the future.

Grouped data — if one customer appears in many rows, all of that customer's rows should land in the same set, or the model is tested on people it's already seen. scikit-learn has GroupShuffleSplit for this, and TimeSeriesSplit for repeated time-aware splits. And always set random_state — without it, every run shuffles differently, and you can't tell whether a score change came from your improvement or just a different split.

To recap: train to learn, validate to choose, test once to confirm. Stratify when the target is imbalanced, split by time when predicting the future, and keep groups together. Next up, lesson 8: data leakage, the quiet mistake that breaks the wall between these sets.
